Hinder
HIN-der
v.t.
From Anglo-Saxon hindrian, to keep back, from hinder, behind. Webster 1828: to stop or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to impede. Paul surrenders a right rather than hinder the gospel, and Peter says a husband can hinder his own prayers.

Biblical Definition

Paul had an apostolic right to material support and refused to use it, giving one reason: we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:12). The right was real, and he laid it down because exercising it might have obstructed the message. Peter applies the same verb to the domestic life of a Christian husband, with a consequence that should stop any man reading it: ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7). How a man treats his wife determines whether his prayers get through. Our Lord charges the lawyers with hindering others from an entrance they themselves declined: ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52). And Paul asks the Galatians the question a runner’s coach asks: Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth? (Galatians 5:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HINDER as to stop, or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to impede; to embarrass; to retard or check.

expand to see more

HINDER, v.t. — To stop, or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to interrupt.

To impede; to retard; to check in progressing.

To prevent; to keep back; with from.

HINDER, a. — That is behind; posterior; as the hinder part of a ship.

Anglo-Saxon hindrian, from hinder, behind.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 9:12 — "If others be partakers of this power over you, are not we rather? Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ."

1 Peter 3:7 — "Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered."

Luke 11:52 — "Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered."

Galatians 5:7 — "Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?"

Modern Corruption

1 Peter 3:7 attaches a man’s prayers to his treatment of his wife, which is a far harder complementarianism than either its critics or some of its advocates describe.

expand to see more

The verse is often read only for the phrase the weaker vessel and then argued about. Its actual weight falls elsewhere. Peter commands husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge — to study them, not merely to lead them — to give them honour, and to regard them as heirs together of the grace of life, which is a statement of full spiritual equality in the same sentence as the ordering. And he attaches a sanction that has no parallel: a man who fails here will find his prayers hindered. The headship this dictionary holds (Ephesians 5:22-33; 1 Timothy 2:11-15) is defined by texts like this one, and it is the opposite of the caricature its critics attack and of the entitlement some of its advocates practise. The man bears the heavier accountability, and God will not hear him while his wife is dishonoured.

1 Corinthians 9 is the neglected half of the argument about Christian liberty. Paul spends the chapter establishing his rights — to support, to lead about a wife, to forbear working — and then says he has used none of them, lest the gospel be hindered. The reasoning is not that the rights were doubtful but that a right may be surrendered when its exercise would obstruct the message. This cuts against the reflex, common in a rights-conscious age and now common in the church, of treating every legitimate liberty as a thing to be defended wherever it is questioned. Romans 14 makes the same point about the weaker brother. Liberty is real, and it is precisely because it is real that it can be laid down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek egkope (G1464), a cutting in, an obstruction; egkopto (G1465), to cut into, to impede; koluo (G2967), to forbid or prevent; anakopto, to beat back.

expand to see more

Greek egkope (G1464) — a cutting in, an obstruction placed in a road; lest we should hinder the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12).

Greek egkopto (G1465) — to cut into or impede; that your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7) and who did hinder you (Galatians 5:7).

Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid, to hinder; them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52).

Greek sunkleronomos (G4789) — joint-heir; heirs together of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right, power; the right Paul declined to use (1 Corinthians 9:12).

Usage

"Lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:12) — a real right laid down because its use might obstruct."

"That your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7) — a man’s prayers tied to his treatment of his wife."

"Ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52) — the key taken away by those who would not use it."
